note: Says the theory must be wrong, rambles about a man with his back against it, then loops on equal shares giving both the highest and lowest possible energy.
Blames the sun's own irregular attraction and heterogeneous matter, calls gravitation unproved, then loops on motion round an axis.
Says the stone is drawn steadily down by gravity and falls with astonishing velocity once the brake is released, checked only by air and friction.
Says the stone with greater momentum descends first and that velocity is measured by the weight of the stone.
A list of 'what about the nature of X' questions that collapses into 'the nature of the nature of' repeated.
Talks about light entering the eye equally from every direction as a universal property of matter; nothing on light speed or a medium.
Says the mistake is cohesion rather than gravitation, rambles about atoms and molecules, then loops on the result of a motion repeated many times.
Catechism about a boy, a man and a sled going to the ground, repeated to the end.
Says the fall is the aggregate of many small gravitational forces acting through the distance; never engages with weight vanishing.
Textbook scraps on the weight of water and air and a cube of wood experiment, then repeats the weight of a cubic foot of air.
Says the scale records the velocity of the fall and a difference between the weight he loses and the elevator's weight; no reading of zero.
Reads elevator as a grain elevator, catechism on wheat weight, then repeats 'the difference in the elevator is called the difference in the elevator'.
Restates both cases and says the pressure in the carriage comes from the vehicle's motion rather than his own weight; never links that to gravity or acceleration.
Says you feel seized, thrust along and drawn by the same pull that governs every stone; gravity an invisible universal force; no weightlessness.
Says the scale's index points to a large number, the work done, twenty tons or more.
Says the stone, released from the chain of gravity, drops with force, like a stone from a window.
Says the elevator stays at rest and the scale keeps reading the weight of the elevator and load carried by the cable.
Says the man has been killed, then a railway conductor lecture on drunkards that repeats itself.
Defends equal sharing and blames the assumption that a light wave has one frequency along the ether.
Says equal distribution is unjustified and energy is confined to a few vibrations in particular directions; no frequency dependence or mechanism.
Nonsense about weighing the elevator every quarter hour, the man killed, grain and cloth in a mill; cannot be read as an answer.
Restates that the falling man feels no weight, then muddles about weight distributed over distance and diminished by velocity; no common principle.
Says feather, stone and man all fall alike under a universal pull we cannot resist; never says what is felt.
Says a great jar, fatigue and headache, then a sensation catechism repeating 'I feel it'.
Repeats the prompt's question back as questions, then a hay weights-and-measures catechism.
Says during the fall the feet press downward with increasing force as velocity grows; the carriage man is dragged back by his own weight.
Attributes the wandering to an Almighty hand and a combination of forces, asks whether gravity applies at all; no unseen planet.
Says energy is transmitted gradually through the ether rather than shared, then claims light speed varies with wavelength; no high-frequency point.
Says foot of the mast and that the stone moves with the vessel, but also says a little ahead and wanders into the ship turning twenty degrees.
Says it falls somewhat behind the mast, or ahead, and later ahead of the centre of gravity; not at the foot.
Muddle about inertia, air resistance called gravity and horizontal components; says the man falls with the car and is destroyed; nothing on what is felt.
Says in both cases one's own weight does not act at departure but is overcome by other bodies pressing; no link to acceleration or gravity's nature.
Treats the scale as recording the stress of the cable breaking and the forces of the descent; never says what it reads.
Says the stone falls and strikes the floor with force, and the man's weight bends the floor beneath him.
Says equal sharing is a fiction and energy diminishes, being spent elsewhere in heat and conduction; nothing about high frequencies.
A row of ones, then a clock catechism repeating one question about the pendulum.
Says the scale and man are free to fall, then loops on 'in the state of gravity the earth is in the state of gravity'.
Attributes the deviations to compounded forces, the sun, the planet's inertia and the resistance of a medium; no unseen body.
Contradicts itself, saying gravity is withdrawn when the cable breaks yet gravity alone carries the elevator down; nothing on what is felt.
Calls the theory unscientific for ignoring heat, then loops on the ether being large in one direction and small in another.
Says the Earth's rotation is a constant quantity, then textbook scraps with figure captions and 2pi; no account of the null result.
Moralises about human nature and the brain in a fall; says the carriage man feels only the motion; no common principle.
First says foot of the mast, then calls that erroneous and has the wind carry the stone forward.
Asks questions back, then an insect lesson catechism repeating 'THE BEETLE'.
Blames Uranus's own atmosphere pressing on a surrounding gaseous medium.
Says the theory confuses vibration energy with heat and energy is divided by atomic constitution, then energy conservation talk; no frequency point.
Says the scale records the total change of motion as the cable parts and the sum of a man's exertions; no reading given.
Says the falling man has no idea of gravity and gravity is not true of a small cabin falling, then loops on a garbled law of falling bodies.
Says the stone falls obliquely with a dip, glides along the deck and even strikes the water; never says where it lands.
Says the Earth's motion is not in the direction of light so there is no difference, then nonsense numbers and parabolas.
Attributes the wandering to Uranus's own internal restless energy and rotation, explicitly rejecting a pull from distant bodies.
Says the two stones fall simultaneously and strike with equal velocity, but the reasoning is garbled and even says greater weight gives greater velocity.
Says the fall is gradual and gentle and gravity a continuous uniform force; nothing on feeling weightless.
Says the stone falls with astonishing velocity and is thrown upon the floor while the man struggles.
Says Uranus is incandescent and its irregularities come from the sun's heat reflected from the earth; planets do not obey gravitation.
Hedges between light from Arcturus, a multitude of small bodies around Uranus, and an unnamed unseen force.
Proposes a magnetism in Uranus's own centre and an unrecognised force beyond Newton; no unseen body.
Answers 'Nothing' then repeats the prompt verbatim to the end.
Talks about rays sharing the same radius and the motion of the eye or medium at that instant; nothing on why the speeds match.
Mechanical muddle about the cage, rope and friction heating; never says what is felt.
Assumes the stone strikes the floor and rambles about velocities from different heights; 'a weight we cannot weigh' goes nowhere.
Rambles about cannon-ball angles, sphericity and colours from the Earth's rotation; no account of the null result.
Hedges that weight is not felt in the fall or only in part, says weight is felt only when its direction is altered; muddled, confuses the two cases, no explicit gravity-acceleration link.
Opens 'it is the force which prevents the body from falling', then invents repulsive and attractive gravitation and loops on dividing weight into parts.
Treats the scale as a beam balance yielding gradually to weight and the momentum of the fall; no reading given.
